transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-14 15:00 PST
Duration: ~50 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Oliver Park (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood CSM), Samir Patel (Nimbus ML), Laura Kim (Nimbus Infra), Diego Alvarez (Nimbus SRE), Jade Thompson (Nimbus Product)

Auto Summary (auto-generated, may be noisy):
- Reviewed latest TTFT and streaming traces from last week's pilot run.
- Observed microburst-induced TTFT spikes at p99 tied to kernel selection on the 32k-seq path.
- Kernel-swap to the low-latency stitch reduced median TTFT; small regressions at p99 for long-seq requests.
- Agreed on a 2-hour dedicated benchmark and to collect arrival traces from Nimbus.

Topics: TTFT results, streaming handshake, sequence-length routing, kernel selection, caching behavior, next steps

Transcript (timestamps are approximate, transcription may include errors):
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): yeah thanks everybody for joining, quick checkin we promised to review the microburst results from last Friday, oliver you have the deck?
[00:14] Oliver (Redwood): I do, uh just gonna share screen, bear with me. um so high level we ran three variants: baseline (hosted l7 default kernel), kernel-swap low-latency stitch, and an aggressive quantized fp16 path.
[00:30] Samir (Customer): quick q before you start, when you say stitch kernel is that the stitch-kernel or the stich one that had the prefetch? sometimes the names get swapped in our notes.
[00:41] Oliver (Redwood): yeah sorry nomenclature oops — it's the "stitch" path, the one that prioritizes continuous batching and reduces tokenization overhead, also does a lighter KV-copy for prefix hits.
[00:54] Laura (Customer): cool ok thanks.
[00:57] Oliver (Redwood): so slide one, median TTFT: baseline p50 ~420ms, stitch p50 ~270-290ms, quantized p50 = 260ms but with slightly higher variance.
[01:15] Diego (Customer): did you control for cold KV cache hits on that run? our traffic has a lot of unique prefixes so cache hit rates are low, we worry those numbers are optimistic.
[01:27] Oliver (Redwood): good call. for the microburst sim we used a mixed prefix distribution with about 18% prefix-hit, we also ran a cold start sweep — that's slide 3. cold p50 for stitch was 340ms, baseline 510ms.
[01:43] Samir (Customer): ok that helps. what's the p95/p99 story? we care about worst-case tail given SLAs.
[01:49] Oliver (Redwood): p95 baseline was 880ms, stitch 520ms, quantized 610ms. p99 baseline ~1.8s, stitch ~1.2s but we saw a cluster of long requests at 2.4s tied to very long seqlen (24k-32k) where the stitch path had a temporary scheduling stall.
[02:13] Maya (Redwood): can you explain that stall in plain english? is it an NV kernel queuing thing or runtime scheduling?
[02:20] Oliver (Redwood): it's mostly runtime scheduling with our current continuous-batch windowing. when many long sequences arrive mid-burst, the scheduler attempts to coalesce them but kernel selection for long seqlen picks the high-throughput kernel which has higher startup overhead; stitch chooses low-latency kernel but if a long request sneaks in, stitching the KV and resharding causes a micro pause. transcription note: "resharding" sometimes becomes "re-sharing" in logs.
[02:44] Jade (Customer): so essentially some combo of seq len and arrival pattern breaks the fast path?
[02:48] Oliver (Redwood): yes. in short, short sequences, stitch is great. for mixed heavy tails we hit an oscillation - scheduler flips between kernels and that adds 100-700ms bursts.
[02:58] Priya (Redwood CSM): are we seeing any correlation with container spinups or autoscaling events? could be infra noise.
[03:05] Diego (Customer): we patched our node rotation last week, but there were 2 autoscaler scale-ins during the 90min run at 2:15am which may coincide. i'll check that window.
[03:16] Oliver (Redwood): thanks diego. we purposely pinned the benchmark to a dedicated pool to avoid noisy neighbors but auto-scaler behavior on customer infra can still influence if you're routing through dedicated in your VPC tests.
[03:29] Samir (Customer): ok next curious about streaming handshake — i saw notes about reducing the first chunk latency. what's the delta?
[03:36] Oliver (Redwood): we made two changes: reduced the initial framing from 80ms to 20-30ms by shortening the proto handshake and enabled streaming early-flush on the stitch path. result: first byte time improved by ~60ms median, p95 improved ~120ms. however that increases token churn on microbursts if early-flush triggers too often, causing slightly higher cost per request.
[04:02] Samir (Customer): hm cost tradeoff. rough numbers?
[04:05] Oliver (Redwood): estimated increase of 3-6% token compute for high-burst patterns, but for low-latency sensitive queries you'd see lower user-facing latency.
[04:15] Laura (Customer): for our SLA we need p95 first-token < 800ms during business hours; does that hold in these tests?
[04:23] Oliver (Redwood): with stitch + handshake changes and small batch sizing we hit p95 ~480-520ms on daytime-shaped traces. but again long-tail with 32k seqs still bumps p95 higher in a mixed tail run.
[04:36] Maya (Redwood): so tradeoff framing: smaller batches and stitch + early flush gives us great p50/p95 for regular traffic, but introduce instability for extreme-long sequences unless we bias routing by seqlen.
[04:48] Samir (Customer): can you route by seqlen today? we could forward long requests to the high-throughput kernel and keep short ones on stitch.
[04:56] Oliver (Redwood): yes we have sequence-length aware routing but current thresholds are conservative. we recommended implementing a fast path for <=4k tokens, a mid path for 4k-16k, and a high-throughput path for >16k. the tuning knob is the eligibility window and sampling threshold.
[05:12] Diego (Customer): what about preemption? if a long request is queued and then a burst of short ones appear, can we preempt?
[05:20] Oliver (Redwood): we support preemptive steering at the runtime layer but there's a cost: aborting partially-started kernel work wastes cycles. better to route proactively by predicted seqlen. also we can do micro hedging: launch a low-priority fast-path duplicate for predicted short ones and cancel if the long one is real — but that costs more.
[05:40] Samir (Customer): predictive routing needs good seq-length estimation. our product sometimes streams user input gradually so the full seqlen isn't known up front.
[05:50] Maya (Redwood): right that's common. two mitigations we've used: 1) conservative default routing until prefix length passes X tokens, 2) fast speculative start for the first chunk then switch kernel if longer context arrives. both have tradeoffs.
[06:05] Jade (Customer): out of scope but curious how quantization affected quality — did you run any evals?
[06:11] Oliver (Redwood): we ran quick ngram/perplexity on a small eval set — quantized fp16 had tiny regresses (couple % on some hallucination metrics), not huge but visible. for Nimbus use-case we recommended sticking to fp16 for latency-sensitive non-regulatory paths and keep fp32 for high-fidelity workflows.
[06:32] Samir (Customer): ok that matches our instincts.
[06:35] Maya (Redwood): real quick can we review the specific microburst trace where p99 spiked to 2.4s? oliver do you have the trace id?
[06:43] Oliver (Redwood): yes trace id nf-1211-burst, i'll paste it in chat. (chat paste noise) the trace shows a 0.9s queuing event after a kernel swap at t+0.6s.
[06:58] Laura (Customer): i'm looking at our infra logs and there's a kube-proxy restart at nearly the same time, so maybe correlation not causation.
[07:06] Diego (Customer): yeah i'll correlate the timestamps, could be that the kube restart caused a short spike in network latency which confused the runtime.
[07:14] Priya (Redwood CSM): actionable items then: ricap, can we run a dedicated 2-hour TTFT microburst benchmark with customer-shaped traces and no infra restarts, and also run a variant where we pin scheduler to aggressive seq-aware routing?
[07:29] Oliver (Redwood): yep we can do that, we'll run: baseline, stitch+early-flush, stitch+seq-routing, stitch+seq-routing+quant. collect p50/p95/p99 TTFT, first-byte streaming times, CPU/GPU kernel occupancy and scheduler logs.
[07:44] Samir (Customer): great. also please include the cost delta per 1M requests estimate for each configuration so we can reason about price/perf.
[07:53] Oliver (Redwood): will do.
[07:55] Maya (Redwood): on the security side, laura any blockers for us running perf probes from your VPC?
[08:03] Laura (Customer): we need to open a ticket for egress rule exception for the staging IPs and get compliance signoff. i'll take that.
[08:11] Maya (Redwood): perfect thanks.
[08:13] Samir (Customer): one more question about observability - can your console surface scheduler decisions per request? that'll help us debug routes that flip.
[08:21] Oliver (Redwood): we're adding a per-request routing field in the trace export, currently in beta but we can enable it for your workspace for the run. it will show kernel choice, batch window, and prefix-hit flag.
[08:33] Diego (Customer): that will be super helpful.
[08:36] Maya (Redwood): ok high level recap: run 2-hour dedicated benchmark (Redwood), customer provides 48h traffic sample, laura opens egress ticket, redwood enables per-request routing traces and shares raw logs, then follow up on Monday with results and pricing delta.
[08:53] Jade (Customer): thanks all.
[08:55] Maya (Redwood): any other questions?
[08:58] Samir (Customer): none from me.
[09:00] Maya (Redwood): cool we'll send notes, action items and schedule the demo for 12/21. thanks everyone.
